competitors.name: iink Payments

Contractors who opt in can get funds advanced in 1-2 business days. Serves homeowners, contractors, public adjusters, attorneys and servicers. Pricing is $45-375/mo subscriptions, 2-3% for instant transfers, and a mortgage-processing fee of 1% of check value capped at $299-329 (https://iink.com/pricing). Holds money-transmission licensing via Avidia Bank.

result.white_space:
The generic layer of the idea (servicer packet preparation, chasing, inspection booking, and contractor advances) is already served. iink does it with venture funding and real scale, and CoPayee does the packet piece cheaply with AI. What the sources do not show anyone serving:
1. Homeowner-side management of total-loss, whole-house rebuilds (roughly $300K-$3M). These run over 6-18 months with permit-gated milestones, licensed-contractor verification, state-statutory conditional and unconditional lien waivers, and draw-by-draw servicer inspections. iink's pricing and deposit limits ($100K-$1M) and its subscription model are built around restoration and repair contractors, public adjusters and attorneys pushing many checks. CoPayee stops at endorsement.
2. Owner-protective verification: independent checks that milestone photos, permits and waivers match the payout requested, so the homeowner does not pay for work not done. Servicer inspectors only protect the servicer's collateral. Nothing found sells this to homeowners.
3. Regulator and executive escalation. Newsom's July 2026 directive and the DFPI complaint portal make a documented escalation dossier newly valuable, and no competitor advertises it.
4. Neutral trust position. iink and any contractor-paid model are contractor-aligned, and a homeowner advocate taking fees from contractors carries a conflict of interest.
The window is narrow. iink could add total-loss features, and regulatory pressure on servicers could shrink the pain.
result.evidence_of_demand:
Pain is well documented and current.
- KNX/Audacy reports mortgage companies holding Eaton and Palisades survivors' insurance money in escrow, with contractors reluctant to start. It cites 120+ complaints to the state and a public adjuster working pro bono: https://www.audacy.com/knxnews/news/local/the-latest-roadblock-eaton-and-palisade-fire-survivors-mortgage-companies
- Governor Newsom, 14 July 2026, warned lenders they are adding 'unnecessary red tape' by slowing disbursement of insurance funds during construction, and directed DFPI to collect complaints: https://www.gov.ca.gov/2026/07/14/governor-newsom-warns-that-lenders-must-provide-timely-and-fair-payouts-to-la-fire-survivors/ and https://bcsa.ca.gov/newsroom/2026/07/20260716.html
- The AP story (via union-bulletin) describes survivors 'demoralized' because servicers withhold escrowed rebuild money, including moved goalposts and redundant inspections: https://www.union-bulletin.com/news/national/fire-survivors-were-finally-ready-to-rebuild-homes-a-new-barrier-is-leaving-them-demoralized/article_759b96a7-0269-5f66-b224-558f935fef77.html
- California's 2025 loss-draft laws (AB 495, 2% interest on held funds; AB 493) and the United Policyholders guide show the problem is recognized (https://uphelp.org/claim-guidance-publications/getting-your-mortgage-company-to-release-insurance-proceeds/). Servicers typically release 1/3, 1/3, 1/3 with 7-14 day inspection waits and 5-14 days added per packet correction (https://www.copayee.com/blog/how-to-get-mortgage-company-to-endorse-insurance-check).
Willingness to pay is proven, but at lower price points than the idea assumes.
- iink raised $12M and lists paid plans, with a mortgage-processing fee of 1% of check value capped at $299-329 (https://iink.com/pricing).
- CoPayee charges $49 per homeowner claim and $199-499/mo for contractors and adjusters (https://www.copayee.com/faq).
- Public adjusters take about 10%.
Caveats: no evidence found that homeowners will pay $1,500-3,000 for draw management, or that contractors will pay 1.5-2.5% per draw when iink's advance and instant-transfer fees are 2-3%. Web search budget ran out before I could check Reddit and forum threads, so direct consumer complaints beyond the news coverage are unverified.
result.kill_reason: n/a. Not dominated: iink is a funded direct competitor with real scale, but it targets restoration-claim check flow and does not evidently cover total-loss whole-house rebuild draw management, owner-side fraud protection or regulator escalation. It is crowded on the generic loss-draft admin and contractor-advance layer. It survives only if repositioned to the narrower wedge below.
result.sharper_angle:
Do not build a general loss-draft concierge, because iink and CoPayee already do the packet, chase and advance. Build the homeowner's owner's-representative for total-loss rebuilds. Concretely:
1. Serve only mortgaged total-loss rebuilds above about $300K, where the servicer requires 3-6 inspection-gated draws over 12+ months.
2. Sell independent draw verification as the product: match milestone photos, permits, contractor license and statutory lien waivers against each requested payout, and give a go/no-go recommendation. Nobody sells this to homeowners, and it also makes servicers' inspectors happier.
3. Add a regulator-ready escalation dossier (timeline, servicer commitments and misses, DFPI complaint package), timed to the July 2026 Newsom directive.
4. Drop the contractor-paid acceleration fee at the start. It conflicts with the advocate role and duplicates iink's advance. Charge the homeowner a flat success-based fee, and partner with iink or a lender for advances instead of competing on them.
5. Distribute through channels rather than ads: public adjusters (who lack this skill and would refer the second fight), Eaton Fire Survivors Network, Altadena Land Initiatives, and the free LA County and state rebuild programs.
6. Also consider a B2B2C variant: white-label surge draw capacity for servicers, who are under regulatory pressure to expand capacity. Assurant and OSC are incumbents there, so test it second.
Validate first by checking with 5 LA survivors whether they would pay $1,500+ for verification-plus-escalation, and by testing whether iink's Pro tier actually handles $500K+ multi-draw rebuilds. If it does, the wedge is thinner than it looks and the idea should be dropped.

result.white_space:
The as-written product is mostly built. Signal 1 (phone line-type and age) is a commodity API. Signal 2 (registry, EIN and domain checks) ships in Snappt KYB via Middesk, Renter Inc. and Two Dots. Signal 3, the network moat, is what Findigs (400-500K units) and VERO Fraud Shield (reused phones and addresses flagged across customers) already sell. Findigs also sells to 100-3,000-unit operators, which overlaps most of the 50-5,000-unit target. The remaining white space is narrow and structural.

1. Every network I found is a walled garden inside one vendor's customer base. Findigs sees roughly 400-500K units and VERO sees its own customers. A ring that hops between screening vendors or PMS platforms defeats each one. I found no vendor-neutral, cross-vendor entity registry. That is the actual ISO ClaimSearch analogy, but it is a data-consortium play sold to and through vendors, not a per-application Chrome extension sold to PMs.
2. Managers under about 100 units are served only by bundles, such as TurboTenant plus Snappt, or by manual phone calls. Findigs starts at about 100 units and Snappt sells annual enterprise contracts. That tail is real but low-revenue, and $149 per month from a tiny PM with almost nothing to contribute makes the cold start hard.
3. The verticals the idea lists as later customers are only partly open. Auto lending has Point Predictive (650+ members). Buy-here-pay-here dealers, gig and platform onboarding, and small-balance lenders have no comparable employer/reference-entity consortium that I found, but I did not verify that thoroughly.
4. No competitor I found publishes intelligence on the fraud-service supply side. The employment-verification-for-hire operations with actors answering HR lines are described in the trade press, for example (https://www.leaserunner.com/blog/how-to-spot-fake-landlord-references). This could be tracked as its own threat-intel feed of the businesses selling the lie.

Caveats. My web search budget ran out before I could run the last vendor checks (RealPage, Yardi, Entrata, TransUnion network features, Middesk-style APIs). PMS incumbents could already have or add this. The FCRA claim that entity-only data 'sidesteps' consumer-reporting rules is optimistic, because phone and email tied to applicants used for eligibility decisions tends to be treated as consumer-report data. Findigs and VERO handle this as internal fraud flags inside their own platforms.
result.evidence_of_demand:
Demand for fraud tooling is strong and already paid for. Demand for a new cross-vendor registry specifically is unproven: I found no forum, RFP or survey asking for one.

- Fraud is prevalent. The NMHC/NAA survey reports 93.3% of large operators experienced fraud in the prior 12 months, 84.3% saw fabricated pay stubs, employment references or income documents, and 80% saw applicants misrepresent application information. Source: NMHC, https://www.nmhc.org/news/press-release/2024/rampant-increasing-fraud-impacting-rental-housing-costs/ (as summarized in search results; the full page did not load for me), plus https://www.nmhc.org/research-insight/research-report/nmhc-pulse-survey-analyzing-the-operational-impact-of-rental-application-fraud-and-bad-debt/.
- Most fraud is caught late. More than 70% of operators did not catch it until after move-in (search-result summary of the NMHC survey). The 2025 Snappt fraud rate was 5.1% of 1.46M submissions, with 'template farms' accounting for 42,600+ cases. Source: https://natlawreview.com/press-releases/snappt-releases-2026-multifamily-fraud-report-revealing-how-applicant-fraud-is-scaling-across-the-industry. 61% of property managers say they lack confidence in preventing fraud.
- Money is flowing. Findigs closed a $32M Series C (June 2026, $80M total, https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2026/06/02/3305372/0/en/findigs-raises-32m-series-c-funding-to-redefine-leasing-decisioning.html). Snappt has raised about $152M. 100 bought Cobblestone Labs in June 2026 (https://siliconangle.com/2026/06/09/rental-screening-startup-100-acquires-fraud-detection-firm-cobblestone-labs/).
- PMs already spend on employer and landlord verification. Snappt sells employer phone and email verification and KYB. Renter, Inc. has sold rental-history verification since 2015 to named PM customers (https://www.renterinc.com/).
- The consortium model sells. Point Predictive has 650+ lender members (https://pointpredictive.com/press-releases/point-predictives-fraud-consortium-surpasses-650-financial-institutions-protecting-over-4-trillion-in-loan-originations/).
- The specific attack is documented. Trade sources describe verification-for-hire services with actors answering phones and a local number (https://www.leaserunner.com/blog/how-to-spot-fake-landlord-references), and Snappt's own Landlord Verification page confirms 'friends pretending to be landlords' (https://snappt.com/blog/fake-landlord-references-problem/).
- Weak evidence that information sharing is wanted. Trade coverage says operators believe fraud is a place to make an exception to competitive secrecy (search-result summary of a NAA/NMHC-related query; unverified beyond that). Independent evidence that operators would pay a separate vendor for a neutral registry: none found. Willingness to pay for the idea's specific price of $1.50-3.00 per check or $149-499 per month: none found. Snappt publishes no per-application price.
result.sharper_angle:
Do not build the PM-facing per-application checker with a Chrome extension. Findigs, VERO, Snappt (KYB plus landlord verification), Renter Inc. and Two Dots already cover its three signals, and they sell inside the software PMs already use.

Instead, build the vendor-neutral entity consortium as infrastructure, aimed at the walled gardens' blind spot. Track only entities (phones, emails, domains, EINs, 'landlord' contacts, addresses), never people, and sell the graph as an API and data feed to screening vendors, PMS platforms and small lenders. Suggested first customers are the mid-tier vendors and portals without their own network, such as RentSpree, TurboTenant, Zillow and Buildium-class platforms, plus the non-multifamily verticals Point Predictive does not obviously serve: buy-here-pay-here dealers, gig platforms and small-balance lenders. The pitch is that a ring hopping across vendors defeats any single network, and a neutral pool sees the hops.

Seed it differently from the original plan. Start with a threat-intel feed on the fraud-service supply side: employment-verification-for-hire operations and template-farm sellers, meaning their phone banks, listing sites and domains, sold as a subscription. It needs no PM contributions to start and is what the competitors' blogs describe but do not sell as a feed.

Before committing, run two tests.
1. Ask Findigs, VERO and Snappt whether they would ingest or contribute to a neutral feed. Their incentive is to keep data proprietary, so a 'no' from all three kills the model.
2. Get an FCRA opinion on entity-linked data used in eligibility decisions.

If neither test passes, kill it. A reasonable falsifier: fewer than 3 of 10 vendor or lender conversations lead to a paid pilot.

Nothing below is web-verified. Likely unserved: (1) A sampling-variance-certified referee product, meaning a Gy/TOS-based protocol with a stated sampling variance, heterogeneity characterisation (variography, sampling nomogram) and a binding-settlement clause. Inspection majors sell 'independent sampling and assay' as a commodity service, but I found no evidence that they publish or guarantee sampling uncertainty for black mass. (2) On-site, containerised, inert-atmosphere sample prep at the recycler or gigafactory gate. Black mass is being pushed toward hazardous-waste treatment in the EU, which makes shipping bulk samples to distant labs harder. (3) Tying lot-level sampling data to EU Battery Regulation material-recovery and recycled-content documentation. The main risk is that SGS, Bureau Veritas/Inspectorate, Intertek or Alex Stewart already offer black-mass sampling and umpire assay and would call this an existing service. The whole wedge depends on their protocols being meaningfully worse than TOS practice, which is unproven and is exactly what the free duplicate-sampling study would test.

What I found no one doing:
1. Physical as-built verification. Every competitor works from paper (supplier certificates, BOMs, entity screening). Nobody reconciles installed serial numbers, cell lot codes and nameplates against those certificates. Notice 2026-15 makes the 'knows or has reason to know' standard the crux, and a mismatch between paper and hardware is the strongest red flag.
2. Physical or firmware attestation tied to tax credit deals. The rogue-radio, teardown and RF work exists only as national-lab and government activity. I found no commercial product that puts it into a transfer-buyer or lender file.
3. An independent verifier role, separate from the developer's own software. Buyers currently rely on seller reps, indemnities and counsel opinions. A neutral third party whose evidence format is accepted is unfilled, though the accounting firms are the natural incumbents.

The idea's premise needs correcting. It says IRS cost tables are not due until 2027 and 'nobody can prove compliance'. In fact Notice 2026-15 (Feb 2026) already gives interim safe harbors, allows reliance on Notice 2025-08 cost percentages and sets a certification safe harbor. Updated tables are expected before Dec 31, 2026 and proposed regulations by year-end 2026. The gap is diligence and evidence quality, not the absence of a method. The 'first firm whose methodology is accepted becomes the standard' thesis is also weaker, because accounting firms and Empact are already establishing de facto practice.

- Insurance is not available. Crux says PFE insurance is not yet available and underwriters are waiting for counsel work product. The 'insurers will only underwrite against our record' claim is a hope, not a market.
- The cyber layer is being pre-empted by regulation. The FCC put foreign-produced inverters on its Covered List on July 28, 2026, with federal audits and a DHS/DoD conditional approval path. A Trump directive on Aug 27, 2026 bans foreign-made bulk-power BESS, with DOE implementation due by Dec 24, 2026. Private attestation may become redundant, or may become a niche for the portion of the market outside 69 kV+ bulk-power equipment.

What the fetches show.
1. The filing and calculation layer is crowded and commoditized. That includes ES-003/ACE upload, per-entry eligibility, and CSV batch prep. Free (TariffRefunds.com), flat-fee (TariffRefund, Inc.), 20-40% consultants, brokers with native filing rights, and free CAPE all cover it. CBP's CSV takes entry numbers only. An 8-12% success fee on a task that CBP has made a bare entry-number list is a weak wedge.
2. The wave is largely spent. CAPE launched April 20, 2026 and it is now Sept 29, 2026. Most of the pool, and almost certainly most of the easy small-importer claims, has been filed by brokers, consultants or the importers themselves. What is left is the hard tail, which is the idea's own thesis. That tail is small and legally uncertain.
3. The likely unserved wedge is the claim-diligence and underwriting file for the hard tail, meaning entries liquidated beyond 80 days and other future-phase entries. Buyers of refund claims need chain of title, IOR verification, liquidation and protest timelines, drawback and FTZ overlap checks, and a probability-weighted value tied to the Federal Circuit appeal. Nothing I fetched offers this. The two direct competitors found are filing-focused and neither mentions claim sales, financing or diligence files. Absence on two home pages is weak evidence, though. Claim-buying funds and lenders may already run their own diligence in-house.
4. The route that only exists because of the tail is broker-side software plus buyer-side diligence, not consumer-style filing. Small importers are not a good direct-acquisition segment. The customer is the buyer or lender with claims to underwrite. That buyer has to be validated, and I did not find one.
result.evidence_of_demand:
Partial, and stronger for the filing problem than for the claim-diligence product.

Filing demand. TariffRefund, Inc. is selling to a ~330,000-importer market with a $503K average refund and a waitlist that opened April 20, 2026 (https://www.tariffrefund.com/). Peacock Tariff Consulting and PRAKTIKAI built a free calculator as lead generation for paid consulting (https://www.tariffrefunds.com/). TariffRefund's pricing page says consultants charge 20-40% of the refund (https://www.tariffrefund.com/pricing). That is a competitor's claim and unverified, but it implies importers are already paying large fees for this work. Big importers are litigating directly, for example Nintendo (https://techcrunch.com/2026/03/06/nintendo-sues-the-u-s-government-for-a-refund-on-tariffs/). The Supreme Court ruling of Feb 20, 2026, the CIT refund order of March 4, 2026, and CAPE's April 20, 2026 launch are confirmed on Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Learning_Resources,_Inc._v._Trump). CBP's own page confirms the liquidated-entry cutoff of 80 days, the CSV-only filing, and the restriction that only the IOR or its broker can file (https://www.cbp.gov/trade/programs-administration/trade-remedies/ieepa-duty-refunds).

Claim-trading demand. I found NO verified evidence of buyers paying for standardized diligence files or of hedge-fund and lender claim purchases. The idea asserts these, and I recall press coverage of funds buying refund rights at a discount, but I could not retrieve a source. Wikipedia's article has nothing on secondary markets. Treat this as unverified.
result.kill_reason: n/a. The filing and calculation half is crowded and commoditized (free CAPE, free calculators, flat-fee platforms, brokers with native filing rights). But the claim-diligence and chain-of-title 'data room' half showed no direct competitor in my limited fetches, so I am not killing the idea. That is a weak signal, given that search was unavailable. result.sharper_angle: Drop the small-importer filing product. Filing is now a free or flat-fee commodity, and CBP restricts who can file. Build only the buy-side underwriting layer for the hard tail. That means a diligence file and a probability-weighted valuation model for liquidated and out-of-window IEEPA entries, sold per file ($500-$2,000) to claim buyers, lenders and the law firms and brokers who sell claims to them. result.sharper_angle: Drop the two-sided factory-credential marketplace at the start and do not compete on data. result.white_space:
Caveat on coverage: the WebSearch quota was exhausted (200 of 200) before this task started. I substituted direct WebFetch of competitor pages, Google News RSS, and some Brave and Bing queries. Brave rate-limited me (429) and Bing returned junk. Hoeford and Fios pages were blocked or truncated. So 'nothing found' is weaker than a full sweep, and the founder should confirm with Crunchbase and LinkedIn plus 10 calls to seed VCs.

What I found. Both halves of the idea have adjacent players, but I found no one selling the specific product as described.

Poll half. Expert networks (GLG, Guidepoint, Third Bridge) and scientific-diligence boutiques (Alacrita, Fios) all sell expert input to investors. They interview senior experts and KOLs, sell bespoke projects, and market to finance clients. I found no fixed-price, 5-day, named-claim consensus poll of 8-15 anonymous junior bench scientists. That is a real wedge, and it fits the founder's critique that the incumbents rely on conflicted seniors.

Replication half. 'Wet diligence' at CROs or independent labs is an accepted practice (LifeSciVC says it should be 'gating before investing'). Hoeford appears to sell it. Science Exchange has the marketplace and the history (Reproducibility Initiative, RP:CB). The bundle, where the poll narrows the question and then a pre-registered, blinded replication follows, looks unserved. Owning a bench pool of laid-off scientists is the least defensible and most operationally risky part.

Segment. AI-bio founders building on published wet-lab claims are the least served, but Adaptyv Bio (raised $40M, 3-week assays from $149 per protein) is already serving protein-design validation.

Structural threats.
- GLG or Guidepoint can copy the poll cheaply once it is proven, since they already sell surveys.
- Anonymity is leaky in subfields of 20-50 people.
- Postdocs risk their careers and may breach university confidentiality or employment terms.
- A negative poll about a named PI's paper carries defamation and tortious-interference exposure.
- A replication that fails in a new lab does not prove the claim is false, which is the ambiguity buyers hate.
result.evidence_of_demand:
The problem is real and well documented. Willingness to pay at these price points is not proven.

Problem evidence:
- Amgen confirmed 11% of 53 landmark preclinical cancer studies and Bayer at most about 25% (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Replication_crisis).
- The Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology found effect sizes 85% smaller on average, 70% of experiments needed reagent requests, and no paper's protocol was fully described (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reproducibility_Project). Only 50 of 193 experiments could be repeated. That matches the 'cells cultured as previously described' pain in the idea.
- Freedman et al. 2015 estimated about $28B per year of irreproducible US preclinical spend, with a point estimate of 53% irreproducible (https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371/journal.pbio.1002165).

Investor-side evidence:
- LifeSciVC (a biotech VC) says 'at least 50%' of top-journal studies can't be repeated by an industrial lab. It says independent repetition 'should be gating before investing', and cites a company that burned about $5M validating a platform that didn't exist (https://lifescivc.com/2011/03/academic-bias-biotech-failures/). This shows VCs know wet diligence is needed and already buy it from CROs.

Existing spend on workarounds:
- Alacrita sells KOL-based scientific diligence to pharma and VCs.
- Hoeford markets independent-lab data verification to investors.
- GLG, Guidepoint and Third Bridge sell expert calls and surveys to funds.

Gaps in demand evidence:
- I found no RFPs and no published prices or customers for a poll-only memo or a key-experiment replication.
- The IFP 'Replication Engine' proposal (https://ifp.org/the-replication-engine/) says it found no evidence that funders, industry or investors currently demand replication services. It is a policy proposal for computational replication funded at $9M by NSF, not a commercial competitor.
- Science Exchange had a replication-validation brand in 2012-2017 and no longer markets it, which suggests weak commercial pull for standalone replication.
- The $4-6k and $15-40k price points are untested.
result.sharper_angle:
Launch poll-only and drop the owned replication bench pool, at least at first.

1. Pick one subfield the founder knows, such as CAR-T, organoids or targeted protein degradation. Sell fixed-price 5-day 'practitioner reproducibility confidence' memos on named claims. Frame the output as reported confidence and fragile reagents, never as 'this result is false'. That limits defamation risk.
2. Build the moat as a compounding claim-level ledger. Each poll adds to a proprietary subfield database of which labs' protocols, reagents and lots hold up. Sell it as the $30-60k retainer. Expert networks sell one-off calls and cannot easily match a structured, longitudinal dataset.
3. Make the panel structurally clean. Recruit paid junior scientists outside the PI's institution and collaborator network. Enforce minimum panel sizes and anonymity thresholds. Have a lawyer check university-confidentiality terms.
4. Broker replication instead of owning it. Hand the 'what to test first' plan to Science Exchange or an existing CRO, and to Adaptyv Bio for protein-binding claims. Take a referral or project-management fee. This avoids competing with well-funded infrastructure.
5. Consider AI-bio startups as the first buyer. They have budgets and no conflicted-KOL habit, but they are exposed to Adaptyv-style cheap assay validation for protein claims. Aim at claims that cheap assays can't settle, such as cell and organoid systems and complex protocols.
6. Before building, run the founder's own test. Offer the free poll to three seed funds and get one to pay $5k. That would give the demand evidence I could not find.

Parents deliver milk daily to a cooperative, each litre is credited toward school fees, and the monthly total is deducted as payment. Space AI provides the delivery-tracking platform. Piloted at Tuiyo Secondary School. Tuko coverage: https://www.tuko.co.ke/kenya/counties/580102-uasin-gishu-county-launches-program-parents-pay-school-fees-milk-supplies/ . competitors.name: Twiga Foods

competitors.scale_or_funding: Historically well VC-funded. Techpoint reported it paused Nairobi operations to reset in June 2025 (headline seen only).

competitors.name: Apollo Agriculture / One Acre Fund style input-credit lenders
competitors.what_they_do: Financing, inputs, training and insurance for Kenyan smallholders, repaid from harvest income. They could add grain-for-fees as a farmer retention product, but nothing on their sites suggests it. Their sites give no detail on school fee or grain offtake products.
competitors.scale_or_funding: VC-backed. I did not verify the amounts.

result.white_space:
Nobody I found offers a grain, bean or potato fee-credit ledger for schools. Google News, site fetches and GitHub search turned up no startup, cooperative product or open-source tool that gives standard weigh tickets, SMS receipts and a published reference price. The practice is real but informal, and it is ripe for a trust layer.

Unserved specifics:
(1) Secondary boarding and senior schools in maize, bean and potato zones. Uasin Gishu has taken dairy, and Food4Education owns primary school meals.
(2) Fair valuation and receipts for staples. Principal Kegoro at Nyabisia Secondary (Kisii) says 'we accept them to bring maize or beans, then we value them and receipt them', which is exactly the informal, discretionary step to standardise.
(3) A per-school reconciliation of in-kind credit against arrears lists. Zeraki Finance and SchoolPay show no in-kind receipt type.
(4) Linking fee credit to the school's own kitchen demand, so the grain never needs to be sold on.

Risks that shrink the white space:
(a) The supply-side tender and AGPO piece is weak. IDRC reports only 1-2% of AGPO opportunities reach women, youth and disability-owned firms, with 90-day-plus payment delays and kickback demands. Schools buy 65% from brokers by manual tender.
(b) 2026 is a maize shortage year. The deficit is about 5.4M bags, flour is at KES 153-163 per 2kg, and 53% of smallholders cite lack of surplus. Farmers may hold grain back, and valuation disputes will be sharp.
(c) Tickets for day schools are small. The proposed day-school fee is KES 7,675, against KES 53k-88k for boarding.
(d) One entity being fee-credit collector and tender supplier to the same school invites a conflict-of-interest problem.
(e) Storekeepers and brokers benefit from the current opacity.
(f) Absence from news is not proof of absence. WebSearch was exhausted and Crunchbase and Product Hunt were blocked, so a stealth or very small pilot cannot be ruled out.
result.evidence_of_demand:
Strong on problem and informal behaviour. Weak on willingness to pay a platform.

Customers already do this informally:
- Nyabisia Secondary School, Kisii, Sept 2026. The principal says the school accepts maize or beans and 'we value them and receipt them', and also firewood and casual labour, while Form Four students stay away over unpaid fees: https://educationnews.co.ke/form-four-candidates-yet-to-report-to-school-in-kisii-as-national-exams-approach-says-worried-principal/
- The Star, May 2026: rural schools traditionally accept in-kind payments (maize, beans). The eCitizen mandate that would have blocked this was struck down in April 2025 and the ruling upheld in Nov 2025: https://www.the-star.co.ke/news/2026-05-07-ruto-defends-ecitizen-school-fees-policy
- Daily Nation, 2022: 'Ainabkoi school embraces barter trade to settle school fees': https://nation.africa/kenya/counties/uasin-gishu/ainabkoi-school-embraces-barter-trade-to-settle-school-fees-3805622 (403-blocked, headline only).
- West Pokot governor Lonyangapuo asked schools to accept goats, chicken and food as fees, with no valuation system: https://educationnews.co.ke/lonyangapuo-asks-schools-to-accept-barter-trade-in-settling-school-fees/
- Uasin Gishu government built a formal dairy version, 'Maziwa ni School Fees', which validates the model and shows government appetite: https://educationnews.co.ke/uasin-gishu-county-launches-innovative-maziwa-ni-school-fees-programme/

Cash pressure on schools:
- Capitation shortfall. Schools received only 56% of expected capitation by Term 2 2026, and the per-learner deficit is KES 4,905 (received 17,339 of 22,244): https://eastleighvoice.co.ke/education/374040/parents-oppose-proposed-secondary-school-fee-hike-call-for-timely-release-of-capitation-funds and https://eastleighvoice.co.ke/education/339135/second-term-begins-monday-amid-deepening-school-funding-crisis
- Principals in Nation coverage say 'we are still drowning in debt': https://nation.africa/kenya/news/education/-schools-drowning-in-debt-as-term-1-nears-end--5385870
- Principals want fees raised to up to KES 87,781 for national boarding schools: https://www.money254.co.ke/post/fees-in-secondary-schools-rise-to-ksh87k-in-proposed-funding-model-news

Food cost pressure:
- Food and beverage inflation was 8.6% in June 2026, and planners are told to model +10% food costs. The article recommends home-grown school meals linked to local farmers: https://educationnews.co.ke/food-security-pressure-why-kenyan-schools-must-rethink-their-2027-budgets/
- Only 22.8% of smallholders reach the school feeding market, and 65% of school purchases go to traders and brokers via manual tender. In that study 50.5% of farmers said prices did not match the market: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/public-health/articles/10.3389/fpubh.2024.1476888/full
- The School Feeding Bill and the KES 7.8-12.7bn annual funding need show policy momentum for local sourcing (People Daily article was 403-blocked, so I relied on The Star summary): https://www.the-star.co.ke/news/2026-08-26-ruto-at-4-school-feeding-how-far-has-the-promise-gone

No direct evidence of schools paying for such a platform. I found no RFPs, forum complaints about valuation, or paid software for in-kind receipting.
result.sharper_angle:
Drop the two-sided broker-replacement and AGPO tender play from the wedge. It is thin-margin, hits the documented AGPO payment-delay and kickback problems, creates a fee-collector-and-supplier conflict of interest, and puts you against Food4Education and entrenched brokers. Start with the trust layer: a 'Fee Credit Ledger' for boarding secondary and senior schools in maize, bean and potato zones such as Kisii, Nyamira, Bungoma and Trans Nzoia.

Product:
- A standard weigh ticket (scale photo, moisture reading, grade).
- A published reference price, for example the NCPB indicative price or county average, with a transparent handling deduction.
- An SMS receipt to the parent.
- A weekly school-side reconciliation that ties in-kind credit to the arrears list.
- A board of management sign-off flow, so principals get an audit trail and cover against unapproved-levy accusations.

Route to market:
1. Sell it as a module to schools already on Zeraki or SchoolPay, or partner with them, rather than competing on fee collection. That turns the biggest substitution risk into a channel.
2. Copy the 'Maziwa ni School Fees' playbook for staples. Pitch a county government or a county cereals or SACCO structure to run 'Mahindi/Maharagwe ni School Fees' as a sibling programme, since dairy is already taken and county governments have shown they will fund this.
3. Let the school consume the grain it receives (credit at the reference price, delivered to the school kitchen). That avoids tender bids, AGPO and the conflict-of-interest issue in phase one, and it is the direct bridge to the School Feeding Bill's home-grown sourcing agenda.

Revenue: per-learner per-term ledger fee (KES 50-100) or a small handling percentage, with hermetic storage credit as an add-on. Add tender supply and receivables or arrears financing only after the ledger produces data.

Pilot design:
- 2026 is a maize deficit year. Include beans and potatoes, and let parents choose the cash or commodity settlement option.
- Target boarding schools first, because day-school fee tickets (about KES 7,675) are too small.
- Time the pilot for Term 1 2027 and the Nov-Dec 2026 procurement planning window.

competitors.name: Carefull
competitors.what_they_do: Financial safety platform for older adults and families (account monitoring, ScamCheck message analysis, identity and credit monitoring). It is sold B2B2C through banks, credit unions and wealth firms as a member benefit. Partners named on the site include Synovus, Merck FCU, C&N Bank, OceanAir FCU and Edward Jones. It has a US-based care team 7 days a week, and consumers pay $29.99 per month if the institution does not cover it. It is the closest match on buyer, pitch and channel, but it is monitoring plus support rather than a real-time call-back verification line.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Founded 2019, New York. Backed by Commerce Ventures, TTV Capital, Bessemer Venture Partners, Montage Ventures and Fin Capital. The site does not give the round size or the number of institution partners.

competitors.name: Scamnetic
competitors.what_they_do: AI scam detection (KnowScam, Scan&Score, IDeveryone) plus a 24/7 US-based Scam Hotline for scam resolution and victim services. It says it serves banks, credit unions and other financial institutions. I could not confirm white-labelled hotline pricing or named credit union customers.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Not disclosed on the pages fetched.

competitors.name: EverSafe
competitors.what_they_do: Monitors bank, investment and credit accounts for suspicious activity, with trusted-contact alerts and US-based 24/7 fraud support staff. Users can forward suspicious emails for expert review. It sells to banks, credit unions and advisors (Raymond James and Key Financial are named).
competitors.scale_or_funding: Funding not found. The company is established, with a lifetime price guarantee and $1M identity theft coverage.

competitors.name: AARP Fraud Watch Network Helpline
competitors.what_they_do: Free helpline at 877-908-3360, Mon-Fri 8am-8pm ET, staffed by trained fraud specialists and volunteers. It gives guidance and support, not investigation or recovery. This is a free substitute for the 'is this a scam?' call, though it is not embedded in a bank workflow and has no safe-word or relative call-back step.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Non-profit, national brand, free to callers.

competitors.name: DOJ National Elder Fraud Hotline
competitors.what_they_do: Free hotline (833-372-8311), Mon-Fri 10am-6pm ET, for people 60 and older. Case managers help victims report fraud and connect to resources. It is aimed at after-the-fact reporting, not real-time pre-payment verification.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Federal program (DOJ Office for Victims of Crime).

competitors.name: Pindrop
competitors.what_they_do: Voice deepfake detection and caller authentication for bank and credit union contact centers. It protects the institution's inbound calls, not the member's own phone, so it is a different side of the call. It shows that banks and credit unions spend real money on voice-clone fraud.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Enterprise scale. Says it serves 14 of the top 20 banks, and MSUFCU is a named credit union customer.

competitors.name: Hiya
competitors.what_they_do: AI voice detection and spam call protection sold mainly to mobile carriers (Telenor, DNA, Vodafone UK), plus consumer apps (Hiya AI Phone, Spam Blocker). It is automated and not sold to credit unions. It is a substitute for the 'AI detector' route, which the idea argues against.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Established company with carrier deployments in several countries.

result.white_space: Nobody I could verify sells the specific mechanism in this idea. It has four parts: (1) a real-time pre-transaction pause line the senior calls when someone is pressuring them; (2) a live out-of-band check that includes a pre-registered family safe word and a call-back to the real relative through a stored circle; (3) a teller workflow that warm-hands a member making a large cash withdrawal or wire to that line, with the credit union's flag visible to the desk; and (4) in-person enrollment at branches and senior centers. Carefull, EverSafe and Scamnetic sell monitoring, alerts, message checking and after-the-fact victim support. AARP and DOJ run free reporting or advice lines that sit outside any bank workflow. Pindrop and Hiya are automated detection. The unserved piece is an outsourced 'intervention desk' that small credit unions ($300M-$5B) cannot staff themselves, with a documented human check at the moment of the withdrawal or wire. Caveat: this is a thin wedge. Carefull's care team or Scamnetic's hotline could add a call-back script quickly, and the free AARP line is a real substitute for the pure 'is this a scam?' call. The wedge only holds if the value sits in teller integration, the family call-back and the audit trail. A generic hotline will not hold it.
result.evidence_of_demand: Partial. Positive signals: (1) Credit unions and banks already pay for or offer elder-fraud protection as a member benefit. Carefull lists Synovus, Merck FCU, C&N Bank, OceanAir FCU and Edward Jones (https://www.getcarefull.com), and EverSafe and Scamnetic also sell to credit unions and banks (https://www.eversafe.com, https://www.scamnetic.com). (2) Carefull has raised VC money (Bessemer, TTV, Commerce Ventures, Fin Capital, Montage) on this B2B2C model. (3) Institutions spend on voice-clone defense. Pindrop says it serves 14 of the top 20 banks and MSUFCU (https://www.pindrop.com/solutions/). (4) Free human lines with real call volume exist, AARP at 877-908-3360 and DOJ at 833-372-8311, which shows people want to talk to a human about a suspicious contact (https://www.aarp.org/money/scams-fraud/helpline/, https://ovc.ojp.gov/program/stop-elder-fraud/providing-help-restoring-hope). (5) The UK PSR requires 50:50 reimbursement of authorised push-payment fraud between sending and receiving firms, which is the regulatory direction the idea cites (https://www.psr.org.uk/our-work/app-scams/). (6) The CFPB publishes dedicated tools for banks and credit unions on elder exploitation (https://www.consumerfinance.gov/consumer-tools/educator-tools/resources-for-older-adults/). Not verified: the FBI figure of about $352M in AI-linked losses among people over 60 in 2025. The IC3 PDF was unreadable through the fetch tool. I found no evidence of any credit union paying $3-6 per enrolled member per month for a live call-back line, and no evidence that US rules make credit unions liable for authorised scam transfers. The free AARP and DOJ lines cap what a $12 per month direct-to-family tier can charge. Research limit: the session's WebSearch budget (200 calls) ran out before I could run the planned searches. Coverage of funded startups (Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt), RFPs, forum complaints and open-source tools is therefore incomplete, and other competitors may exist.
result.sharper_angle: Do not sell a general 'scam hotline' or a monitoring app. Carefull, EverSafe, Scamnetic and the free AARP and DOJ lines already cover those. Sell an outsourced 'elder exploitation intervention desk' for community credit unions that cannot staff one. It is triggered at the point of loss: the teller sees a large cash withdrawal, wire or crypto-linked pattern and warm-transfers the member to a trained human. That person runs the safe-word check and a call-back to the real relative, then logs a documented intervention record that helps the credit union with elder-exploitation reporting, member-loss reviews and examiner questions. Price per intervention or as a flat desk fee, not $3-6 per enrolled member, so the credit union pays for saves and the desk's cost stays tied to call volume. Distribute through credit union service organizations (CUSOs), state leagues and core or online-banking providers rather than one CEO at a time. Consider partnering with Carefull or EverSafe as their live human layer instead of competing head-on. Run the 60-day pilot first and record dollars withdrawn, interventions and confirmed scams stopped, because that data is the only proof that a credit union will pay for this and not use a free hotline.
